raw_text: I would say I learn a lot and I learn kinda fast compared to before that I learn by my self but cs102 a bit unpredictable like I not sure what it gonna be on exam like If you just do diy you can’t do quiz hard questions for sure like there is noway the guy that can do it is guy that 100+ leetcode and can do hard leetcode questions but main point is it is hard not becuase it really hard but it because it not gradually increases harder and I would say I got better than other because I got good mentor like P.philix is good at teaching compare to other room but that also make it not stable but I not sure how to make it better I feel like Ai can already teach you all If you don’t know and a lot of tool but I feel like it can be better than this like cal1 and intergral 1 I feel like I listen then practice then I can actually do it but programming it just a but confuse especially it start with java .it kinda complicated to start (If you really don’t know anything ) compare to python but yeah I kinda get professors that java is get more salary than python.
points: I learn a lot faster now than when learning by myself, but CS102 is unpredictable regarding what will be on exams. The main issue with CS102 is not that the material is inherently too hard, but that the difficulty does not gradually increase, making standard DIY exercises insufficient for hard quiz questions unless a student has extensive experience like doing 100+ hard LeetCode questions.

I performed better in CS102 because I had a good mentor (like P.philix, who is good at teaching compared to other classrooms), but relying on individual mentor quality makes the overall course learning experience unstable across different sections.

I feel like AI tools can already teach students almost everything when they don't know something, but the overall course structure could still be improved to support learning better than just relying on these tools.

Learning programming is confusing for complete beginners compared to subjects like Calculus 1 where I can listen, practice, and then do it. Starting programming with Java is complicated for beginners compared to Python, though I understand the professors' reasoning that Java leads to higher salaries.
